practice.stem: Crunchy Bites Ltd launched a new range of baked lentil snacks two years ago. Sales are now rising quickly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'product life cycle'.
parts.answer: The stages a product goes through from its introduction to the market until it is withdrawn (introduction, growth, maturity, decline).
parts.working: 1 mark: stages a product passes through over time; 1 mark: from launch/introduction to decline/withdrawal (or naming the stages).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the stage of the product life cycle the lentil snacks are most likely to be in, and state one feature of this stage.
parts.answer: Growth stage; e.g. sales rising quickly / profits starting to rise / competitors begin to enter.
parts.working: 1 mark: growth. 1 mark: a valid feature of growth (rapidly rising sales, profit begins, more distribution outlets, competitors appear).

practice.stem: Mango Fresh sells fruit juice in cartons through shops and school canteens in Punjab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two functions of packaging for Mango Fresh.
parts.answer: 1. Protects the juice from damage and keeps it fresh during transport to canteens. 2. Attracts customers with bright colours and the brand name, helping it stand out on shop shelves. (Also: gives information, e.g. ingredients and expiry date; easy to carry/drink from with a straw; helps brand image.)
parts.working: For each of two functions: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to fruit juice/Mango Fresh.

practice.stem: Hamza makes handmade leather wallets in Lahore. Each wallet costs Rs 240 to make. He uses cost-plus pricing with a mark-up of 25%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of one wallet.
parts.answer: Rs 300

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other pricing methods Hamza could use.
parts.answer: Any two: competitive pricing, penetration pricing, price skimming, promotional pricing, dynamic pricing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: FarmFresh Eggs has a poultry farm near Rawalpindi. It sells eggs to wholesalers, to supermarkets and directly to households.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two channels of distribution.
parts.answer: Any two: manufacturer → consumer (direct); manufacturer → retailer → consumer; manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer; manufacturer → agent → wholesaler/retailer → consumer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correctly described channel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two reasons why FarmFresh Eggs might sell directly to households.
parts.answer: 1. No middlemen take a share of the price, so it earns a higher profit per tray of eggs. 2. Eggs reach customers fresher and the farm gets direct feedback; it can build loyalty with regular home deliveries.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to eggs/FarmFresh.

practice.stem: Spice Route is a new restaurant opening in Faisalabad. The owner wants to attract customers in the first month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two aims of promotion.
parts.answer: Any two: inform customers about a new product; persuade customers to buy; create/improve brand image; increase sales or market share; remind customers about the product.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two methods of sales promotion Spice Route could use.
parts.answer: 1. Opening discount, e.g. 20% off all meals in the first week, to encourage people to try it. 2. Loyalty card: a free meal after five visits, encouraging repeat visits. (Also: free starters/dessert, buy-one-get-one-free, competitions, free samples at a mall stall.)
parts.working: For each of two methods: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to the restaurant. Do not accept advertising methods such as TV or newspaper adverts.

practice.stem: Sialkot Sports Ltd makes cricket bats and sells them under its own brand name in Pakistan, the UK and Australia.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'brand'.
parts.answer: A unique name, symbol or design that a business uses to make its product different from those of competitors.
parts.working: 1 mark: name/symbol/logo/design; 1 mark: distinguishes the product from competitors' products.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Sialkot Sports Ltd of having a strong brand.
parts.answer: 1. Customer loyalty: players who trust the brand buy again and recommend it, so sales are more stable. 2. Higher prices: a respected brand used by famous cricketers allows a premium price, raising profit per bat. (Also: easier to launch new products such as pads under the same brand; easier to enter new countries; retailers more willing to stock it.)
parts.working: For each benefit: 1 mark identify, 1 mark application to cricket bats/Sialkot Sports, 1 mark development of the effect on sales/profit.

practice.stem: Tea Time biscuits have been sold in Pakistan for 25 years. Sales have stopped growing and several rival brands sell similar biscuits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two extension strategies Tea Time could use.
parts.answer: 1. New flavours or varieties (e.g. cardamom or chocolate-filled): attracts new customers and gives existing customers a reason to buy more, so sales rise again. 2. New market, e.g. exporting to the Gulf where many Pakistani workers live, or selling smaller cheap packs in rural shops: reaches customers who have not bought before. (Also: new packaging, new advertising campaign, price reduction, new uses.)
parts.working: For each strategy: 1 mark identify, 1 mark application to Tea Time, 1 mark explanation of how it extends the maturity stage / increases sales.

practice.stem: ZetPhone is launching a new high-quality smartphone in Pakistan with features that no rival phone has yet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'penetration pricing'.
parts.answer: Setting a low price when a new product is launched to attract customers and gain market share quickly; the price may be raised later.
parts.working: 1 mark: low price; 1 mark: at launch / to gain market share quickly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think price skimming is the best pricing method for ZetPhone's new smartphone? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Skimming suits a new, unique, high-quality product: early adopters who want the latest technology will pay a high price, which helps recover development costs and gives a premium image. But rivals may soon copy the features, many Pakistani consumers are price-sensitive, and a high price may limit sales. Judgement: skimming is probably best at first because the features are unique, then lower the price as competitors arrive.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge, up to 2 marks analysis (developed consequences), up to 2 marks evaluation (justified judgement that weighs both sides for this business).

practice.stem:
GlowSkin is a new range of sunscreen made in Malaysia. Its marketing manager has a promotion budget of $40,000 for the launch. Appendix: promotion options.
Option | Cost ($) | Estimated people reached
TV advertising | 36,000 | 900,000
Social media influencers | 12,000 | 400,000
Leaflets | 8,000 | 50,000
Market research shows that 70% of GlowSkin's target customers are aged 16–30.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, recommend which promotion option(s) GlowSkin should use for its launch. Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: TV $0.04; social media $0.03; leaflets $0.16. Social media influencers: cheapest per person ($0.03), and most target customers are 16–30, who use social media most; influencers can show the product being used. TV reaches the most people but uses 90% of the budget and many viewers are outside the target group. Leaflets are expensive per person. Recommendation: influencers, possibly with the leaflets as well (total $20,000), keeping money for later; TV alone leaves little budget.
parts.working: Calculations: Cost ÷ people reached: 36,000 ÷ 900,000 = $0.04; 12,000 ÷ 400,000 = $0.03; 8,000 ÷ 50,000 = $0.16. Content: cost per person reached TV $0.04, influencers $0.03, leaflets $0.16; 70% of target customers aged 16–30 (heavy social media users); TV uses 90% of the $40,000 budget and reaches many outside the target group; leaflets costly per person but local; combinations within budget (e.g. influencers + leaflets = $20,000). Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to GlowSkin, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to GlowSkin, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem: Gul Crafts is a small business in Peshawar that makes hand-carved wooden boxes and sells them at a local market stall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'e-commerce'.
parts.answer: Buying and selling goods or services using the internet (e.g. through a website, app or online marketplace).
parts.working: 1 mark: buying and selling; 1 mark: over the internet / online.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one opportunity and one threat that e-commerce creates for Gul Crafts.
parts.answer: Opportunity: it can sell its boxes online to customers across Pakistan and abroad (e.g. tourists or overseas Pakistanis), not just market visitors, so sales and revenue can rise. Threat: customers can easily compare prices with other woodcarvers and factory-made boxes online, so Gul Crafts may have to cut prices; also delivery costs and breakages, and it needs IT skills.
parts.working: Opportunity: 1 identify + 1 application + 1 development. Threat: 1 identify + 1 application + 1 development.

practice.stem:
Kool Kola is a soft drink made by Riverside Drinks plc. Appendix: annual sales (thousand bottles).
Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Sales | 5 | 18 | 45 | 70 | 74 | 72

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in sales from Year 3 to Year 4. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the stage of the product life cycle Kool Kola has reached in Year 6. Use the data to support your answer.
parts.answer: Maturity (possibly saturation / start of decline): sales have levelled off at about 72–74 thousand and fell slightly from Year 5 to Year 6.
parts.working: 1 mark: maturity/saturation. 1 mark: evidence from the data (sales growth stopped; 74 → 72).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how Riverside Drinks' promotion and pricing of Kool Kola are likely to have been different in Year 1 compared with Year 5.
parts.answer: Year 1 (introduction): heavy informative promotion (e.g. launch adverts, free samples) to make people aware of the new drink; price either low (penetration) to win customers or high (skimming) if the drink was unique. Year 5 (maturity): promotion mainly reminds customers and defends the brand against rivals (e.g. loyalty offers, sponsorship); price set competitively, close to rival soft drinks, possibly with promotional discounts.
parts.working: Promotion: 1 mark for Year 1 (informative/awareness, high spending) + 1 mark for Year 5 (reminder/persuasive, defend market share). Price: 1 mark for Year 1 (penetration or skimming, with reason) + 1 mark for Year 5 (competitive/promotional pricing).

practice.stem:
CleanHome Ltd makes three brands of washing powder. The directors want to stop making one brand to free factory space for a new liquid detergent. Appendix (Rs thousand per year):
Brand | Revenue | Total costs | Product life cycle stage
Sparkle | 1,800 | 1,260 | decline
Breeze | 2,400 | 1,560 | maturity
Bloom | 900 | 720 | growth

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, recommend which brand CleanHome Ltd should stop making. Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: Sparkle Rs 540 thousand; Breeze Rs 840 thousand; Bloom Rs 180 thousand. Sparkle is the likely choice: it is in decline, so its profit of Rs 540 thousand will probably keep falling. Bloom makes the least profit now (Rs 180 thousand) but is in growth, so profits should rise as sales grow and launch costs fall. Breeze is the most profitable and mature, so keeping it gives a steady income. Dropping Sparkle loses some profit in the short term, but its customers might switch to Breeze or the new liquid detergent.
parts.working: Calculations: Revenue − total costs: Sparkle 1,800 − 1,260 = 540; Breeze 2,400 − 1,560 = 840; Bloom 900 − 720 = 180 (Rs thousand). Content: profit Sparkle Rs 540 thousand, Breeze Rs 840 thousand, Bloom Rs 180 thousand; profit margins (Sparkle 30%, Breeze 35%, Bloom 20%); product life cycle stages — decline means falling future profit, growth means rising profit as launch costs fall; customers may switch to other brands or the new liquid detergent. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to CleanHome Ltd, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to CleanHome Ltd, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem: SkyLite is a new low-cost airline that will fly between Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad and Dubai. It competes with larger, well-known airlines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'marketing mix'.
parts.answer: The four main elements a business uses to market a product: product, price, place and promotion (the 4Ps).
parts.working: 1 mark: elements/decisions used to market a product; 1 mark: names product, price, place, promotion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two elements of the marketing mix that are important for SkyLite. Which element is likely to be the most important? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Price: as a low-cost airline its main appeal is cheaper fares than the well-known airlines, attracting students and families who would otherwise travel by road. Promotion: as a new brand nobody knows it, so it must advertise its fares (e.g. on social media) to win customers. Judgement: price is most important, because low fares are its unique selling point; promotion only works if the fares really are lower, and a basic product is acceptable to price-sensitive passengers.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge of two elements; up to 2 marks analysis applied to SkyLite; up to 2 marks evaluation choosing the most important with a reason why it beats the other.

practice.stem: Two businesses in Islamabad are each thinking of raising prices by 10%. Fuel Point is the only petrol station on a busy motorway for 60 km. Bean There is one of eight cafés on the same street.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'price elastic demand'.
parts.answer: When a change in price causes a proportionally larger change in quantity demanded.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantity demanded changes; 1 mark: by a larger percentage than the price change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the 10% price rise is likely to have a different effect on the revenue of Fuel Point and Bean There.
parts.answer: Demand for Fuel Point's petrol is likely to be price inelastic: drivers need fuel and there is no nearby alternative, so quantity falls by less than 10% and total revenue rises. Demand for Bean There's coffee is likely to be price elastic: there are seven close substitutes, so many customers switch and quantity falls by more than 10%; total revenue falls. So Fuel Point may raise its price; Bean There probably should not.
parts.working: Fuel Point: 1 mark inelastic, 1 mark reason (necessity / no substitutes nearby), 1 mark revenue rises. Bean There: 1 mark elastic, 1 mark reason (many substitutes), 1 mark revenue falls.

practice.stem:
Natura is a new business in Lahore making organic face cream. It must choose one channel of distribution for its first year. Appendix:
Option A – sell online direct to consumers: price Rs 1,200, delivery cost Rs 150 per jar, website and online advertising Rs 1,500,000 a year, expected sales 8,000 jars.
Option B – sell to pharmacies and beauty shops (retailers): they pay Rs 800 per jar, expected sales 20,000 jars.
Option C – sell to a wholesaler: it pays Rs 650 per jar, expected sales 35,000 jars.
Each jar costs Rs 500 to make.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, recommend which channel of distribution Natura should choose for its first year. Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: A: Rs 2,900,000; B: Rs 6,000,000; C: Rs 5,250,000. Option B: highest expected profit (Rs 6.0 m), and pharmacies give a trusted image for a skincare product; customers can see and test it. Option C gives high volume but the lowest profit per jar (Rs 150) and Natura loses control over where it is sold and how it is displayed. Option A has the best margin and direct customer contact but the lowest profit because of website costs and uncertain online demand for a new brand. B is best for year one, perhaps adding online sales later when the brand is known.
parts.working: Calculations: A: (1,200 − 500 − 150) × 8,000 − 1,500,000 = Rs 2,900,000. B: (800 − 500) × 20,000 = Rs 6,000,000. C: (650 − 500) × 35,000 = Rs 5,250,000. Content: expected profit A Rs 2.9 m, B Rs 6.0 m, C Rs 5.25 m; profit per jar (A Rs 550 before website costs, B Rs 300, C Rs 150); control over display and image, trusted pharmacy image for skincare, direct customer contact online, risk and reliability of sales forecasts for a new brand. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Natura, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Natura, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem: RideNow is a ride-hailing app in Karachi. It uses dynamic pricing: fares rise automatically when many people request rides at the same time, for example during rain or rush hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage to RideNow of using dynamic pricing.
parts.answer: Higher fares at busy times encourage more drivers to work then, so more ride requests are met and RideNow earns more revenue when demand is highest.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies advantage (higher revenue/profit at peak times or matches supply of drivers to demand). 1 mark: explanation linked to RideNow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think dynamic pricing will help RideNow increase its profits in the long term? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Yes, it raises revenue at peak times and keeps drivers available, improving service. But customers may feel cheated by very high fares during rain or emergencies, damaging the brand; with rival apps they may switch, and bad publicity or government action could follow. Judgement: it helps profits if price rises are limited and explained clearly in the app; very large rises could cost loyal customers.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge, up to 2 marks analysis (developed consequences), up to 2 marks evaluation (justified judgement that weighs both sides for this business).

practice.stem: Fit Zone plans to open a gym for women in Quetta.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'primary research'.
parts.answer: Collecting new (first-hand) information for a specific purpose, e.g. by questionnaires, interviews, observation or focus groups.
parts.working: 1 mark: new/original/first-hand data; 1 mark: collected by or for the business for its own purpose (or method example).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two sources of secondary research Fit Zone could use.
parts.answer: Any two: government statistics (e.g. population census), internet/websites, newspapers and magazines, market research agency reports, competitors' websites or price lists, trade association reports.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A bakery chain in Colombo, Sri Lanka, wants to know whether customers would buy a new range of sugar-free cakes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two methods of primary research the bakery could use.
parts.answer: 1. Questionnaire: customers in the shops answer set questions about whether they would buy sugar-free cakes and at what price. 2. Product testing / free samples (or focus group): customers taste the cakes and give their opinions before full launch. (Also: interviews, observation, online survey.)
parts.working: For each of two methods: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to the bakery.

practice.stem: Pixel Print is a small business in Kampala, Uganda, that prints T-shirts. It wants to find out what designs young customers prefer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of using an online questionnaire for this research.
parts.answer: Any two: cheap; quick to reach many people; young people use social media so it reaches the target market; results are easy to analyse automatically; can include pictures of designs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of using an online questionnaire for this research.
parts.answer: Any two: low response rate; people who answer may not be representative; cannot ask follow-up questions; people may give careless answers; some people may answer more than once.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: FrostyCream asked 400 people outside one shopping mall in Lahore which new ice-cream flavour they would buy. 92 chose mango, 140 chose pistachio, 108 chose chocolate fudge and 60 chose none of these.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of people asked who chose mango.

parts.label: b
parts.text: FrostyCream estimates that 25,000 people in its target market will buy a new flavour. Using the results for pistachio, estimate how many of them would choose pistachio.
parts.answer: 8,750 people

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the results of this survey may not be reliable.
parts.answer: 1. Sample from one mall only: shoppers there may be wealthier or younger than the whole target market, so results are biased. 2. People may say they would buy a flavour but not actually buy it, or answer quickly to get away. (Also: sample size small relative to market; leading questions; time of day/season.)
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark identify + 1 mark explain linked to FrostyCream.

practice.stem: Bolan Travels runs coaches between Quetta and Karachi. It plans to start a premium service with reclining seats and Wi-Fi. The marketing manager must choose between an online survey sent to 2,000 past customers by email and a focus group of 10 regular passengers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems Bolan Travels might have in making sure its market research is accurate.
parts.answer: 1. The sample may not represent the target market: past customers who gave an email address may be younger or richer than other passengers, so the results could overstate demand for the premium service. 2. Questions may be badly written or leading, or people may not answer honestly about how much extra they would pay, so the firm could set the wrong fare. (Also: low response rates; out-of-date data; researcher bias.)
parts.working: For each problem (max 4 each): 1 mark identify; 1 mark apply to Bolan Travels' premium coach service; 2 marks explain the consequence for its decision.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend which research method Bolan Travels should use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Online survey: cheap, quick and gives numerical data from many people, so the firm can estimate how many would pay more; but response rates may be low and answers are short. Focus group: gives detailed opinions on seats and Wi-Fi and why people value them, but only 10 people, so may not represent all passengers. Recommendation: the online survey, because the key question is how many customers would pay the higher fare; a focus group could follow to refine features.
parts.working: Content: online survey of 2,000 — cheap, quick, numerical data on how many would pay more, but low response rate and short answers; focus group of 10 — detailed opinions on seats and Wi-Fi and why, but small and may not represent all passengers; the key question is how many would pay the higher fare; a focus group could follow. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Bolan Travels, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Bolan Travels, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks.

practice.stem: Leila wants to open a bookshop and café in Muscat, Oman. She has limited money for research and plans to rely only on secondary research.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two pieces of information secondary research could give Leila.
parts.answer: e.g. population/age structure of the area; average incomes; number and locations of competing bookshops/cafés; trends in reading or café spending; rents in the area.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two relevant pieces of information.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think secondary research alone is enough for Leila? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Secondary research is cheap and quick and shows market size, incomes and competitors. But it was collected for other purposes, may be out of date and will not tell her what local customers want from a bookshop-café (e.g. Arabic or English books, prices, opening hours). As a new business with limited money, a mistake would be costly, so a small amount of cheap primary research (e.g. a short questionnaire to people in the area or a social-media poll) is worthwhile. Judgement: not enough on its own.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge, up to 2 marks analysis (developed consequences), up to 2 marks evaluation (justified judgement that weighs both sides for this business).

practice.stem: HealthyBite plans to sell a new protein bar. An online survey of 1,200 gym members found that 60% would buy the bar at Rs 150 and 25% would buy it at Rs 200. Each bar costs Rs 90 to make.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should HealthyBite rely on these survey results to choose the price of its protein bar? Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, the expected profit per 1,000 gym members at each price).
parts.answer: Calculations: Rs 150: Rs 36,000; Rs 200: Rs 27,500. The results suggest Rs 150 gives more profit (Rs 36,000 v Rs 27,500 per 1,000 members) and more customers. But only gym members who use the internet were asked, so the sample excludes other possible buyers; people often say they will buy but do not; answers for one bar per person ignore how often people buy; competitors' prices are not considered. Judgement: use the results as a guide (Rs 150 looks better) but test-market in a few gyms before deciding.
parts.working: Calculations: Rs 150: 600 buyers × (150 − 90) = Rs 36,000. Rs 200: 250 buyers × (200 − 90) = Rs 27,500. Content: per 1,000 gym members, Rs 150 → 600 buyers × Rs 60 = Rs 36,000; Rs 200 → 250 buyers × Rs 110 = Rs 27,500; limitations — only online gym members sampled, stated v actual behaviour, frequency of purchase ignored, competitors' prices not considered; test marketing. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to HealthyBite, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to HealthyBite, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem: Cool Breeze sells air coolers in Pakistan. Last year its sales were Rs 360 million and total market sales of air coolers were Rs 2,400 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Cool Breeze's market share.
parts.working: Market share = firm's sales ÷ total market sales × 100 (M1) = 360 ÷ 2,400 × 100 = 15% (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'market segment'.
parts.answer: An identifiable sub-group of a whole market in which consumers have similar characteristics or needs.
parts.working: 1 mark: part/sub-group of a market; 1 mark: customers with similar characteristics (e.g. age, income, location).

practice.stem: Velocity Sportswear sells trainers and sports clothing in Pakistan and the UAE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'niche market'.
parts.answer: A small, specialised segment of a larger market with particular needs.
parts.working: 1 mark: small part/segment of the market; 1 mark: specialised/particular needs (e.g. running shoes for marathon runners).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways Velocity Sportswear could segment its market.
parts.answer: 1. By age: different ranges for children and adults, so designs and prices can match each group and advertising can be aimed at them. 2. By use/lifestyle (activity): football boots, running shoes, gym wear; customers needing specialist products will pay more. (Also: income, gender, location/region, e.g. lighter fabrics for the UAE climate.)
parts.working: For each way: 1 mark identify, 1 mark application to sportswear, 1 mark explanation of the benefit (better targeting, higher sales).

practice.stem:
Desi Chips Ltd sells potato crisps. The managing director is pleased that sales have increased. Appendix (Rs million):
Year | Desi Chips sales | Total market sales
Year 1 | 4.2 | 30
Year 2 | 4.6 | 40
Two new foreign crisp brands entered the market in Year 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Desi Chips' market share in each year. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the managing director should be concerned, and explain one way Desi Chips could respond to the new competition.
parts.answer: Sales rose by about 9.5% but the market grew by a third, so market share fell from 14.0% to 11.5%; rivals, including the new foreign brands, are growing faster and Desi Chips may lose bargaining power with shops. Response: e.g. launch new local flavours (e.g. chatpata masala) that foreign brands do not offer, and promote them, to attract customers and win back share; or improve distribution to small shops in rural areas.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks: concern explained using data (sales up but share down, market growing faster, new entrants). Up to 3 marks: one response identified, applied and developed.

practice.stem: Laptop Lane is a computer shop in Rawalpindi. Customers now compare prices online, and two large electronics stores have opened nearby.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways Laptop Lane could keep its customers despite the stronger competition. Which way is likely to be the most important? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: 1. Better customer service: expert advice, installing software and fast repairs that big stores and online sellers do not offer; customers who value help will stay loyal. 2. Loyalty scheme / after-sales care, e.g. discounts on repairs for returning customers. Judgement: customer service is most important, because a small shop cannot match large stores on price, but personal service gives a reason to pay slightly more and creates loyalty and recommendations.

practice.stem: Masala Munch Ltd makes spicy snacks in Karachi. It wants to sell in Malaysia and is considering a joint venture with a Malaysian food company.

parts.working: Advantage: 1 identify, 1 application, 1 development. Disadvantage: 1 identify, 1 application, 1 development.

practice.stem: Sukoon Herbal Teas makes herbal tea in Pakistan. Its advertisements say the tea "cures headaches and stress". It wants to sell in the European Union, where advertising and labelling laws are strict. Option 1: open its own shops in Germany. Option 2: license a German tea company to pack and sell the tea under the Sukoon name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways laws may control Sukoon Herbal Teas' marketing in the European Union.
parts.answer: 1. Laws against misleading advertising: Sukoon cannot claim the tea 'cures' headaches unless this is proved, so its adverts must change, which may weaken its main selling point. 2. Labelling and food-safety laws: packs must show ingredients, weight and allergy information correctly, which may need new packaging and testing and raises costs. (Also: rules on product safety, weights and measures, consumer rights to refunds.)
parts.working: For each way (max 4 each): 1 mark identify the legal control; 1 mark apply to Sukoon's tea or its 'cures' claim; 2 marks explain the effect on Sukoon's marketing or costs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend which option Sukoon Herbal Teas should choose to enter the German market. Justify your answer.

But it loses control of quality and receives only a share of the profit. Own shops: full control and all the profit, but very expensive, slow, and Sukoon lacks local knowledge. Recommendation: licensing at first, with strict quality terms in the contract, because it reduces legal and financial risk in an unfamiliar market.
parts.working: Content: licensing — low cost and risk, German partner knows EU labelling laws and has distribution, royalties, but less control of quality and only a share of profit; own shops — full control and all the profit, but very expensive, slow and lacks local knowledge; strict quality terms in a licence contract. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Sukoon Herbal Teas, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. practice.stem:
Sindh Snacks makes crisps in a factory in Hyderabad. It needs a production supervisor for a shift of 30 workers. Appendix 1 shows the two shortlisted applicants.

practice.stem:

parts.label: a
parts.text: Option B costs $3,900. Which option should CodeNest choose to train its new developers? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: $17,400. Option B is $13,500 cheaper and the training is directly related to CodeNest's own systems and projects; developers keep producing while learning. However, the senior developer's bad habits may be passed on, and his own work suffers. Option A gives expert, structured training and possibly recognised qualifications, but costs more and developers are away for 5 days. Judgement, e.g. Option B because CodeNest's systems are specific to the company, so an outside course may not cover them, and the saving of $13,500 is large.
parts.working: Calculations: cost per person = 850 + 5 × 120 = $1,450. 12 × 1,450 = $17,400. Content: Option A costs 12 × (850 + 5 × 120) = $17,400, so B is $13,500 cheaper; B uses CodeNest's own systems and developers keep working, but the senior developer's output falls and bad habits may pass on; A gives expert, structured training and possibly qualifications, but costs more and developers miss 5 days. practice.stem: Medicare Pharmacies has 40 branches in Pakistan. When a branch manager leaves, head office always advertises the job externally.

parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Medicare Pharmacies should always recruit branch managers externally? Justify your answer.

parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

practice.stem: Chenab Weaving in Faisalabad plans to buy automated looms costing PKR 30 million. The new looms would replace 40 workers. Each worker earns PKR 45,000 per month, and each would receive a redundancy payment equal to 3 months' pay. The new looms would cost PKR 9 million a year to run and maintain.

parts.text: Should Chenab Weaving buy the automated looms? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.

Looms may also improve quality and output. Against: large outlay may need a loan; remaining workers may be demotivated or strike; bad publicity locally; staff need training to use looms. Judgement with reasoning, e.g. buy, because the cost is recovered in about 2.8 years, but communicate with workers and the union first.
parts.working: Calculations: 3 × 45,000 = 135,000 per worker. 135,000 × 40 = PKR 5,400,000. Content: redundancy pay PKR 5.4 m; wage saving 40 × 45,000 × 12 = PKR 21.6 m a year; net saving PKR 12.6 m a year after running costs; total outlay PKR 35.4 m recovered in about 2.8 years; quality and output; loan finance; morale, union action, local reputation, training. parts.answer: Giving a subordinate the authority to carry out tasks or make decisions, while the manager remains responsible.

practice.stem: The manager of a Karachi call centre makes all decisions herself and tells staff exactly what to do.

practice.stem: BrightAds is a small advertising agency in Lahore with 15 creative staff who design advertising campaigns. Its manager currently uses an autocratic style.

parts.text: Identify two features of democratic leadership.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one advantage and one disadvantage to Sialkot Sportswear of paying a piece rate.
parts.answer: Advantage: machinists are encouraged to sew more shirts, which raises output and the business only pays for what is produced. Disadvantage: workers may rush, so the quality of the shirts may fall and more need to be checked or rejected.
parts.working: 2 marks each: 1 for the point, 1 for linking it to Sialkot Sportswear. Other disadvantage: workers' pay is unstable, which may cause stress or staff leaving.

practice.stem: StarLink Contact Centre in Manila, Philippines, has many staff leaving within a year. Staff say the work is repetitive and boring, although the pay is above average.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using Herzberg's theory, explain why the above-average pay is not stopping staff from leaving.
parts.answer: Pay is a hygiene factor: good pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not motivate; staff need motivators such as interesting work, recognition and responsibility.
parts.working: 1 mark: pay is a hygiene factor. 1 mark: hygiene factors only remove dissatisfaction / motivators are missing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two non-financial methods StarLink could use to motivate staff. Which method is most likely to reduce the number of staff leaving? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Job rotation: staff move between tasks (inbound calls, emails, complaints), reducing boredom, but each task may still be repetitive. Job enrichment: staff are given more responsibility, e.g. solving complaints themselves, which gives a sense of achievement (a Herzberg motivator), but needs training. Other: teamworking, training and promotion opportunities, recognition schemes. Judgement, e.g. job enrichment, because the problem is boring work and enrichment adds the motivators Herzberg says are missing, whereas rotation only varies equally simple tasks.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each method (knowledge + analysis). 2 marks for a justified choice that explains why the other method is less effective.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Indus Insurance choose to motivate its sales staff? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: PKR 2,160,000. Option 1: directly linked to sales, so it may raise sales quickly; only paid if targets are met; but costs up to PKR 2.16 m a year, may encourage mis-selling, and the effect fades (Herzberg: money is a hygiene factor). Option 2: cheaper (PKR 0.9 m); satisfies esteem and self-actualisation needs; builds skills that help selling; but the effect on sales is slower and some trained staff may leave for rivals. Judgement with reasoning, e.g. Option 2, because it costs less than half of Option 1 and gives long-term motivation, unless sales must rise immediately.
parts.working: Calculations: 5% × 3.6 m = PKR 180,000 per month. × 12 = PKR 2,160,000. Content: Option 1 costs up to 5% × 3.6 m × 12 = PKR 2.16 m a year, paid only if targets are met, quick link to sales, risk of mis-selling, money as a hygiene factor; Option 2 costs PKR 0.9 m, meets esteem and self-actualisation needs, builds selling skills, slower effect, trained staff may leave. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Indus Insurance, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'internal communication'.
parts.answer: The exchange of information between people within the same organisation.
parts.working: 1 mark: passing information/messages. 1 mark: between people inside the business (e.g. managers and workers).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two barriers to effective communication.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. use of jargon/technical language; poor listening; noise or distractions; wrong medium chosen; message too long or unclear; language differences; long chain of command; poor attitude towards the sender.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The manager of a clothing shop in Quetta uses notices on the staff board and also holds a weekly staff meeting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between one-way and two-way communication.
parts.answer: One-way communication goes from the sender to the receiver with no reply or feedback; two-way communication allows the receiver to reply and give feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of the two methods used by the manager is two-way communication, and give one benefit of using it.
parts.answer: The weekly staff meeting; benefit, e.g. staff can ask questions so the manager can check they have understood / staff can suggest ideas.
parts.working: 1 mark: staff meeting. 1 mark: valid benefit.

practice.stem: SpeedPost, a courier firm, has 400 delivery drivers across Karachi. It must tell all drivers about a change to delivery routes that starts in two days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two elements of effective communication, other than the message itself.
parts.answer: Any two: sender (transmitter); receiver; medium (method used); feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two methods SpeedPost could use. Which method is best? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Text message to phones: reaches all 400 drivers immediately wherever they are, cheap, and gives a written record, but drivers may not read it or have questions. Depot briefing meeting: two-way so drivers can ask about new routes and managers can check understanding, but hard to gather 400 drivers who work different shifts within two days. Judgement, e.g. text messages followed by a short briefing at each depot for questions, because speed matters with only two days and the drivers are spread across the city.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each method (application + analysis). 2 marks for a justified judgement.

practice.stem: Habib Agro Exports has offices in Multan and Hamburg, Germany. Managers in the two offices often misunderstand each other's emails and orders are sometimes sent with the wrong specifications.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two barriers to communication that Habib Agro Exports faces, and suggest how each could be reduced.
parts.answer: 1) Language: emails written in a second language may be unclear; reduce by using simple English, translators, or standard order forms. 2) Distance / time-zone difference: messages wait hours for a reply, so problems are not cleared up; reduce with scheduled video calls during overlapping office hours. Other: technical jargon about produce specifications – use a glossary; no feedback – ask the receiver to confirm the order.
parts.working: For each of two barriers: 1 mark for the barrier, 1 mark for its effect in context, 1 mark for a suitable way to reduce it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one example of external communication for Habib Agro Exports.
parts.answer: e.g. sending an invoice or a price list to a German supermarket customer; emailing a shipping company about delivery dates.
parts.working: 1 mark for a message to someone outside the business; 1 mark for a relevant method/context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which communication method should CareWell Hospitals choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: PKR 1,080,000. Option 1: written record, but one-way, costs PKR 1.08 m a year and news is up to a month old. Judgement, e.g. Option 2, because it is cheaper than the newsletter from the first year and reaches shift workers quickly; urgent policy changes could still be explained at meetings.
parts.working: Calculations: 60 × 1,500 = PKR 90,000 per month. × 12 = PKR 1,080,000. Content: Option 1 costs 60 × 1,500 × 12 = PKR 1.08 m a year, one-way and up to a month old; Option 2 costs PKR 950,000 in year 1 then PKR 150,000 a year, instant, reaches shift workers, allows feedback, but some staff may not check it; Option 3 two-way with questions, but takes staff from patients and messages may differ between wards. practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem: Golden Crust is a bakery in Hyderabad that makes bread and cakes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'fixed costs'.
parts.answer: Costs that do not change with the level of output in the short run, e.g. rent.
parts.working: 1 mark: do not vary with output; 1 mark: short run / example such as rent, salaries, insurance (must be linked).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two variable costs for Golden Crust.
parts.answer: Any two: flour, sugar, eggs, butter, packaging, electricity/gas for ovens (if per batch), wages paid per item.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept rent or managers' salaries.

practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem: Kite Masters makes kites for the spring festival season. Fixed costs are $18,000 per season. Each kite sells for $12 and has variable costs of $7. It expects to sell 5,000 kites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even level of output.
parts.answer: 3,600 kites
parts.working: Contribution per kite = 12 − 7 = $5 (M1). Break-even = 18,000 ÷ 5 = 3,600 kites (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety.
parts.answer: 1,400 kites
parts.working: Margin of safety = expected sales − break-even output (M1) = 5,000 − 3,600 = 1,400 kites (A1).

practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem: Coastal Nets makes fishing nets in Gwadar. Its fixed costs are $50,000 a year and its variable cost is $20 per net. It makes 5,000 nets a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average cost per net.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two economies of scale Coastal Nets could gain if it grew larger.
parts.answer: 1. Purchasing economies: buying nylon thread in bulk gives discounts, lowering cost per net. 2. Technical economies: it can afford faster net-making machines that produce more nets per hour. (Also: financial economies – cheaper loans; marketing economies – advertising cost spread over more nets; managerial economies – specialist managers.)
parts.working: For each of two economies: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to Coastal Nets.

practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem: Oak & Pine makes wooden chairs in Nairobi, Kenya.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether each of these costs is fixed or variable: (i) rent of the workshop, (ii) wood for each chair, (iii) insurance, (iv) paint for each chair.
parts.answer: (i) fixed (ii) variable (iii) fixed (iv) variable
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Monthly fixed costs are $15,000 and the variable cost is $35 per chair. Calculate the total cost of making 600 chairs in a month.

practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem: Desert Rose makes scented candles in Bahawalpur. Each candle sells for Rs 450 and has variable costs of Rs 270. Fixed costs are Rs 900,000 a year. Next year it expects to sell 7,000 candles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected profit next year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even level of output.
parts.answer: 5,000 candles

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one limitation of break-even analysis for Desert Rose.
parts.answer: It assumes all candles made are sold at the same price, but Desert Rose may have unsold candles or give discounts, so actual break-even could be higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: limitation (assumes all output sold / constant price / costs stay constant / straight-line costs / only as good as forecast data). 1 mark: explanation applied to Desert Rose.

practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem: Threadline Ltd is a garment exporter in Faisalabad. In three years it has grown from 80 to 900 workers and opened two more factories.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two diseconomies of scale Threadline Ltd might experience.
parts.answer: 1. Poor communication: with 900 workers across three factories, messages pass through many levels and arrive late or distorted, so mistakes in orders for foreign buyers increase and costs rise. 2. Low worker motivation: workers feel unimportant in a large firm and managers rarely see them, so absenteeism and labour turnover rise and productivity falls. (Also: weak coordination between factories / slow decision-making.)
parts.working: For each: 1 mark identify, 1 mark application to Threadline, 1 mark development showing average costs rise.

practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem: Sun Shade makes garden umbrellas. It sells each umbrella for $80; variable cost is $50 per umbrella and fixed costs are $120,000 a year. It expects to sell 6,000 umbrellas. The manager is considering raising the price to $90, which market research suggests would reduce sales to 5,200 umbrellas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Sun Shade raise its price to $90? Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, the break-even output and expected profit at each price).
parts.answer: Calculations: At $80: break-even 4,000, profit $60,000. At $90: break-even 3,000, profit $88,000. Yes, probably: profit rises from $60,000 to $88,000, break-even falls from 4,000 to 3,000 and the margin of safety rises from 2,000 to 2,200. But the forecast fall in sales may be wrong; if rivals keep lower prices, sales could fall more, and lower sales could cost market share in the long term. Judgement: raise the price if the research is reliable, and monitor sales.
parts.working: Calculations: $80: 120,000 ÷ 30 = 4,000; 30 × 6,000 − 120,000 = $60,000. $90: 120,000 ÷ 40 = 3,000; 40 × 5,200 − 120,000 = $88,000. Content: $80: break-even 4,000, profit $60,000, margin of safety 2,000; $90: break-even 3,000, profit $88,000, margin of safety 2,200; reliability of the market-research forecast; rivals' prices; market share in the long term. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Sun Shade, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Sun Shade, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem: FreshMart has grown from one supermarket to a chain of 40 supermarkets across Pakistan. In its central bakery, output rose from 10,000 loaves a week (total cost Rs 400,000) to 25,000 loaves a week (total cost Rs 750,000).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'economies of scale'.
parts.answer: The factors that cause average (unit) costs to fall as a business increases its scale of production.
parts.working: 1 mark: average/unit costs fall; 1 mark: as output/size of the business increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average cost per loaf before and after the increase in output.
parts.answer: Before Rs 40; after Rs 30

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why FreshMart may be able to charge lower prices than a small corner shop.
parts.answer: FreshMart buys in bulk for 40 stores, so suppliers give large discounts (purchasing economies); it can borrow more cheaply and spread advertising over many stores. Lower average costs mean it can charge lower prices and still make a profit, whereas a corner shop buys in small quantities at higher unit cost.
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant economy identified (up to 2) + up to 2 marks for explaining the link from lower average cost to lower prices, with application.

practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem: Pure Pour bottles mineral water in Murree and sells each case for $25. It must choose a new bottling machine. Machine A: fixed costs $200,000 a year, variable cost $15 per case. Machine B (more automated): fixed costs $320,000 a year, variable cost $9 per case. Expected sales are 30,000 cases a year, but sales vary a lot with the weather.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Recommend which bottling machine Pure Pour should buy. Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, the break-even output and expected annual profit for each machine).
parts.answer: Calculations: A: break-even 20,000 cases, profit $100,000. B: break-even 20,000 cases, profit $160,000. Both break even at 20,000 cases, but above that B earns $16 per case instead of $10, so at 30,000 cases B gives $60,000 more profit. Risk: below 20,000 cases B makes bigger losses (higher fixed costs), and sales depend on weather. Unless sales are likely to fall below 20,000, choose B; it may also need fewer workers, though breakdowns of an automated machine could stop production.
parts.working: Calculations: A: 200,000 ÷ (25 − 15) = 20,000; 10 × 30,000 − 200,000 = $100,000. B: 320,000 ÷ (25 − 9) = 20,000; 16 × 30,000 − 320,000 = $160,000. Content: both break even at 20,000 cases; profit A $100,000, B $160,000 at 30,000 cases; contribution $10 v $16 per case; B's higher fixed costs mean bigger losses below break-even; weather makes sales uncertain; automation — fewer workers, breakdown risk. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Pure Pour, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Pure Pour, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem:
Aroma Kitchenware can make only one new product next year. Appendix:
Item | Rice cooker liner (X) | Pressure cooker (Y)
Selling price ($) | 15 | 40
Variable cost per unit ($) | 9 | 22
Fixed costs ($) | 48,000 | 135,000
Forecast sales (units) | 12,000 | 9,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, recommend which product Aroma Kitchenware should make. Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, break-even output, margin of safety and expected profit for each product).
parts.answer: Calculations: X: break-even 8,000, margin of safety 4,000, profit $24,000. Y: break-even 7,500, margin of safety 1,500, profit $27,000. Y gives slightly more profit ($27,000 v $24,000), but its margin of safety is only 1,500 units (17% of forecast) compared with 4,000 (33%) for X. If sales are 20% below forecast, X still makes a profit (9,600 units → $9,600) but Y makes a loss (7,200 units → −$5,400). X is the safer choice unless the forecast for Y is very reliable; the extra $3,000 profit from Y is small for the extra risk.
parts.working: Calculations: X: contribution $6; 48,000 ÷ 6 = 8,000; 12,000 − 8,000 = 4,000; 6 × 12,000 − 48,000 = $24,000. Y: contribution $18; 135,000 ÷ 18 = 7,500; 9,000 − 7,500 = 1,500; 18 × 9,000 − 135,000 = $27,000. Content: X break-even 8,000, margin of safety 4,000 (33%), profit $24,000; Y break-even 7,500, margin of safety 1,500 (17%), profit $27,000; if sales are 20% below forecast X still profits, Y makes a loss; reliability of forecasts; fit with existing range. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Aroma Kitchenware, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Aroma Kitchenware, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided.
