practice.subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
practice.stem: Sara is opening a small café in Gilgit. Her weekly fixed costs are Rs 42,000. Each meal sells for Rs 600 and costs Rs 250 in ingredients and packaging.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many meals Sara must sell each week to break even.
parts.answer: 120 meals

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think a break-even chart would be useful to Sara when she opens her café? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Useful: shows how many meals she needs to sell (120 a week) and the profit or loss at different sales levels; helps her see the effect of changing prices or costs, and supports a loan application. Limitations: assumes all food prepared is sold and every meal sells at the same price, but cafés waste food and offer different meals; costs (e.g. ingredient prices) change; tourist demand in Gilgit is seasonal, so weekly sales vary. Judgement: useful as a planning guide for a new business, but she should update it and not rely on it alone.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge, up to 2 marks analysis (developed consequences), up to 2 marks evaluation (justified judgement that weighs both sides for this business).

practice.stem: Saba Ceramics makes floor tiles. Last month 40 workers produced 12,000 boxes of tiles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'productivity'.
parts.answer: A measure of the efficiency of inputs: output per unit of input, e.g. output per worker in a time period.
parts.working: 1 mark: output compared with inputs; 1 mark: e.g. output per worker per period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate labour productivity for last month.
parts.answer: 300 boxes per worker
parts.working: Labour productivity = output ÷ number of workers (M1) = 12,000 ÷ 40 = 300 boxes per worker per month (A1).

practice.stem: Three businesses in Lahore use different methods of production.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the most suitable method of production (job, batch or flow) for each business: (i) a tailor making wedding dresses to each customer's design; (ii) a bakery making 200 loaves of brown bread, then 200 loaves of white bread; (iii) a factory filling soft-drink bottles 24 hours a day.
parts.answer: (i) job (ii) batch (iii) flow
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one disadvantage of flow production.
parts.answer: e.g. Very high cost of machinery: the business needs large, steady demand to cover it; or boring, repetitive work lowers worker motivation; or a breakdown at one stage stops the whole line; or products are standardised.
parts.working: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline.

practice.stem: Rehman Rice Mills processes and packs rice in Gujranwala. Its manager wants to increase productivity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two ways Rehman Rice Mills could increase productivity.
parts.answer: 1. Train workers so they operate the husking and packing machines faster with fewer mistakes. 2. Buy more automated packing machines, so more bags are packed per worker per hour. (Also: improve motivation, e.g. bonuses; better organisation/lean production; reduce machine breakdowns with maintenance.)
parts.working: For each of two ways: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to the rice mill.

practice.stem: Sahil Motors assembles cars in Karachi. It is thinking of introducing just-in-time (JIT) inventory control, so that parts arrive from suppliers only when needed on the assembly line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'lean production'.
parts.answer: Techniques used to reduce waste of all kinds (e.g. time, materials, inventory) in production and so increase efficiency.
parts.working: 1 mark: reducing waste; 1 mark: to improve efficiency / lower costs (or examples JIT, kaizen).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of JIT for Sahil Motors.
parts.answer: Advantage: little money is tied up in inventory of parts and less warehouse space is needed, so costs fall and cash is available for other uses. Disadvantage: if a supplier delivers late (e.g. imported parts delayed at the port or by strikes), the assembly line stops, cars are not finished and customers wait, so sales are lost.
parts.working: Advantage: 1 identify, 1 application, 1 development. Disadvantage: 1 identify, 1 application, 1 development.

practice.stem: Chenab Bicycles makes bicycle frames. In Year 1, 60 workers produced 48,000 frames. In Year 2, after new welding equipment was installed, 65 workers produced 54,600 frames.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate labour productivity in each year.
parts.answer: Year 1: 800 frames per worker; Year 2: 840 frames per worker

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in labour productivity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why higher productivity is important for Chenab Bicycles.
parts.answer: More frames per worker means lower labour cost per frame (average costs fall). Chenab can then cut prices to compete with imported bicycles, or keep prices and earn a higher profit margin; it may also afford higher wages, improving motivation.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower average/unit costs. 1 mark application. Up to 2 marks development: more competitive prices, higher profit, higher wages, faster delivery to customers.

practice.stem: Golden Biscuits Ltd makes biscuits using batch production: one oven line makes one type for a few hours, then is cleaned and changed to another type. Demand for its best-selling biscuit has grown so much that the line runs that type nearly all the time. The directors are considering a new flow-production line for this biscuit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Golden Biscuits Ltd of using flow production for its best-selling biscuit.
parts.answer: 1. Lower average costs: machines run continuously without stopping for cleaning and changeover, and ingredients can be bought in bulk, so each biscuit costs less and prices can be competitive. 2. Higher output and consistent quality: an automated line makes identical biscuits quickly, so the firm can meet growing demand without losing sales.
parts.working: For each benefit (max 4 each): 1 mark identify; 1 mark apply to the biscuit factory (changeovers, high demand); 2 marks develop the consequence (costs, profit, meeting demand).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend whether Golden Biscuits Ltd should introduce flow production for this biscuit. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Yes, if demand stays high: the line already runs this biscuit almost constantly, so flow production uses the equipment fully and cuts unit costs. Risks: high cost of the new line; if tastes change, a dedicated line is inflexible; workers may find tasks repetitive. Because demand is large and stable, the cost savings and output are likely to outweigh the risk; keep batch production for the other types.
parts.working: Content: line already runs this biscuit almost constantly, so flow uses equipment fully and cuts unit costs; high cost of the new line; inflexible if tastes change; repetitive work and motivation; keep batch production for other types; level and stability of demand. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Golden Biscuits Ltd, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Golden Biscuits Ltd, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks.

practice.stem: Chiniot Furniture makes hand-carved beds using many skilled craftsmen. Lahore Steel makes steel sheets using large automated rolling machines and few workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between labour-intensive and capital-intensive production, using these two businesses as examples.
parts.answer: Labour-intensive production uses a large amount of labour relative to capital (Chiniot Furniture – skilled carvers, few machines). Capital-intensive production uses a large amount of machinery relative to labour (Lahore Steel – automated rolling machines, few workers).
parts.working: 1 mark each definition (2) + 1 mark each correctly linked example (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two benefits to Lahore Steel of using technology in production.
parts.answer: 1. Higher productivity: machines produce more sheets per hour than workers could, lowering average costs. 2. Consistent quality: computer-controlled machines give the same thickness every time, reducing waste and rejected sheets. (Also: lower labour costs; can operate 24 hours; safer for workers.)
parts.working: For each of two benefits: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to Lahore Steel.

practice.stem: Pak Packaging Ltd makes cardboard boxes. It is considering buying an automated cutting machine costing $500,000. The machine would reduce the number of production workers from 50 to 30. Each worker is paid $12,000 a year. The factory is the main employer in a small town.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual saving in wages and the number of years of wage savings needed to cover the cost of the machine. Give the number of years to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Saving $240,000 a year; 2.1 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Pak Packaging Ltd should buy the automated machine? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: wage costs fall by $240,000 a year, so the machine pays for itself in about 2.1 years; cutting is faster and more accurate, so quality and output improve. Against: 20 workers lose their jobs in a town where the firm is the main employer – bad publicity, lower morale among remaining workers, possible union action; redundancy pay; machine needs maintenance and skilled operators. Judgement: buy it, since the payback is short, but reduce the impact by retraining some workers to operate and maintain the machine or by natural wastage.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge, up to 2 marks analysis (developed consequences), up to 2 marks evaluation (justified judgement that weighs both sides for this business).

practice.stem: Al-Noor Pharmacy controls its inventory of a common painkiller. The maximum inventory level is 900 packs, the reorder level is 400 packs and the buffer inventory is 200 packs. It sells 100 packs a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lead time (the number of days between placing an order and receiving it) if the order arrives just as inventory falls to the buffer level.
parts.answer: 2 days
parts.working: Inventory used during lead time = 400 − 200 = 200 packs (M1). 200 ÷ 100 = 2 days (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many packs should be ordered each time so that inventory returns to the maximum level when the order arrives.
parts.answer: 700 packs
parts.working: Order quantity = maximum − buffer (M1) = 900 − 200 = 700 packs (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one problem for Al-Noor Pharmacy of holding too much inventory and one problem of holding too little.
parts.answer: Too much: cash is tied up and medicines may pass their expiry date and have to be thrown away; storage costs rise. Too little: the pharmacy may run out, so patients go to another pharmacy and it loses sales and goodwill.
parts.working: Too much: 1 identify + 1 explain (opportunity cost of cash, expiry/waste, storage, theft). Too little: 1 identify + 1 explain (stock-outs, lost sales/customers, cannot meet sudden demand).

practice.stem: City Care Hospital's pharmacy often has long queues, and staff spend time searching for medicines on badly organised shelves. The manager wants to introduce kaizen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'kaizen'.
parts.answer: Continuous improvement through many small changes, usually suggested by workers themselves.
parts.working: 1 mark: continuous improvement; 1 mark: small changes / ideas from workers (teams).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think kaizen will improve the efficiency of the hospital pharmacy? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Likely yes: staff know the problems best and can suggest small changes, e.g. reorganising shelves so common medicines are near the counter, labelling, or a separate queue for collecting repeat prescriptions; queues and wasted time fall at little cost, and staff feel valued. But it takes time and needs managers to listen and staff to be willing; it will not solve major problems such as too few pharmacists. Judgement: it should improve efficiency if managers support it and act on suggestions.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge, up to 2 marks analysis (developed consequences), up to 2 marks evaluation (justified judgement that weighs both sides for this business).

practice.stem: Two businesses are choosing where to locate: a clothing shop and a brick-making factory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two factors that affect the location of the clothing shop.
parts.answer: Any two: footfall/number of customers passing; nearness to competitors or other shops; rent; parking/transport access; security; visibility.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two factors that affect the location of the brick-making factory.
parts.answer: 1. Nearness to raw materials: clay is heavy and costly to transport, so a site near clay deposits cuts costs. 2. Availability and cost of land: brick kilns need large areas and are best away from homes because of smoke. (Also: transport links to building sites; supply of labour; planning rules; energy supply.)
parts.working: For each of two factors: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to brick-making.

practice.stem: Thread World Ltd makes T-shirts in a factory in the UK. Its directors are thinking of moving production to Bangladesh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Thread World Ltd might relocate its factory to Bangladesh.
parts.answer: 1. Lower wage costs: garment workers in Bangladesh earn much less than in the UK, so labour cost per T-shirt falls and the firm can cut prices or raise profit. 2. Closer to raw materials and suppliers: cotton fabric and garment suppliers are nearby, lowering transport costs and delivery times. (Also: government incentives/export zones; large workforce with garment skills; avoid UK rules or costs; access to Asian markets.)
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark identify, 1 mark application, 1 mark development.

practice.stem:
Fresh Pack Ltd packs dried fruit for export through Karachi port. It needs a new warehouse with 40 workers. Appendix: annual costs (Rs).
Item | Site A (Hub, inland) | Site B (near Karachi port)
Rent | 1,800,000 | 1,200,000
Wage per worker | 420,000 | 480,000
Transport costs | 2,400,000 | 900,000
Other information: Site A is close to fruit farms in Balochistan; Site B is in a busy industrial area with many skilled workers but traffic congestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, recommend which site Fresh Pack Ltd should choose for its new warehouse. Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: Site A: Rs 21,000,000; Site B: Rs 21,300,000. The costs are very close (A is Rs 300,000 cheaper, about 1.4%), so other factors decide. Site A is near the fruit farms, so fresh supplies arrive quickly and wages are lower, but it is further from the port and transport costs are much higher, and fuel price rises would hurt. Site B is near the port, has skilled workers and lower transport costs, but congestion may delay shipments. Recommendation: either with justification, e.g. B, because export deadlines and skilled packing workers matter more than a 1.4% cost difference, and transport costs are the most likely to rise.
parts.working: Calculations: A: 1,800,000 + 40 × 420,000 + 2,400,000 = Rs 21,000,000. B: 1,200,000 + 40 × 480,000 + 900,000 = Rs 21,300,000. Content: total annual cost A Rs 21.0 m, B Rs 21.3 m (difference Rs 300,000, about 1.4%); A near fruit farms with lower wages and rent v higher transport costs; B near the port with skilled workers and low transport costs v congestion delays; export deadlines; fuel price risk. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Fresh Pack Ltd, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Fresh Pack Ltd, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem:
SolarWave plc makes solar panels in Germany and wants to build a factory in Asia employing 200 workers. Appendix:
Factor | Country P | Country Q
Average monthly wage ($) | 310 | 460
Import tariff on solar panels in that country | 0% | 25%
Government grant for new factories | none | $500,000
Size of local solar market | small | large and growing
Political stability | some unrest | stable

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, recommend which country SolarWave plc should choose for its new factory. Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: $360,000 a year (Q is more expensive). Country Q: although wages cost $360,000 a year more, the grant of $500,000 covers well over one year of the difference; the large, growing market means panels can be sold locally, and making them inside the country avoids the 25% tariff that imported panels would face. Political stability reduces the risk of disruption. Country P has lower wages and no tariff barrier to worry about, but a small market and unrest. Recommendation: Q, because market access and stability outweigh the higher wage bill.
parts.working: Calculations: Difference per worker per month = 460 − 310 = $150; 150 × 12 × 200 = $360,000. Content: wage bill difference $360,000 a year (Q dearer); $500,000 grant in Q covers more than one year of the difference; 25% tariff in Q protects panels made inside Q; large, growing market in Q v small market in P; political stability v unrest. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to SolarWave plc, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to SolarWave plc, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem: BrightCall Ltd plans to open a call centre that answers customer enquiries for banks. It is choosing between a large city and a smaller town where the government offers a tax break to new employers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two factors BrightCall Ltd should consider when choosing the location. Which factor is likely to be the most important? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: 1. Availability of skilled labour: staff need good communication and IT skills; a large city has more graduates, but wages are higher. 2. Government incentives: the tax break in the smaller town lowers costs and raises profit. (Also: reliable internet/electricity, rent.) Judgement: labour is most important, because a call centre's service quality depends on its staff; a tax break is of little use if it cannot recruit enough skilled workers, though if the town has a college the incentive could tip the decision.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge of two factors; up to 2 marks analysis applied to a call centre; up to 2 marks evaluation choosing one with a reason why it beats the other.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways a government might influence location decisions.
parts.answer: Any two: grants or subsidies; tax breaks; planning permission/refusing permission; building infrastructure (roads, internet); special economic zones; laws restricting location (e.g. pollution).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Swat Honey Co. collects, filters and bottles honey for sale in supermarkets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'quality assurance'.
parts.answer: A system of checking quality at every stage of production, so that standards are met and faults are prevented rather than found at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark: checking at every stage of production; 1 mark: to prevent faults/meet agreed standards (involves all workers).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two benefits to Swat Honey Co. of producing high-quality products.
parts.answer: Any two: good reputation/brand image; customer loyalty and repeat sales; can charge higher prices; fewer complaints/returns; less waste; supermarkets more willing to stock it.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The Pearl Hotel in Gwadar has received many online complaints about slow room service, dirty rooms and rude staff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to The Pearl Hotel of introducing total quality management (TQM).
parts.answer: 1. Every member of staff, from cleaners to receptionists, becomes responsible for quality and treats other staff and guests as customers, so problems such as dirty rooms are fixed before guests see them; complaints fall. 2. Better reputation: improved online reviews attract more guests, raising occupancy and allowing higher room rates. (Also: less waste/costs of putting things right; staff more motivated by involvement.)
parts.working: For each benefit: 1 mark identify, 1 mark application to the hotel, 1 mark development.

practice.stem: Hamza Garments makes 25,000 shirts a month. 3.2% of shirts are faulty and must be thrown away; each faulty shirt costs Rs 650 to make. A quality-training course for all workers costs Rs 250,000. The training company says it will reduce the fault rate to 1.4%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Hamza Garments pay for the training course? Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, the number of faulty shirts before and after training and the monthly saving).
parts.answer: Calculations: Before 800; after 350; saving Rs 292,500 per month. Yes: the monthly saving of Rs 292,500 is more than the one-off cost of Rs 250,000, so the training pays for itself in under a month; fewer faults also improve reputation with buyers, and trained workers may feel more valued. But the fault rate of 1.4% is only the training company's claim; workers may forget the training or leave; production time is lost during the course. Judgement: pay for it, as even a much smaller improvement would cover the cost, but monitor fault rates afterwards.
parts.working: Calculations: 3.2% × 25,000 = 800; 1.4% × 25,000 = 350; (800 − 350) × 650 = Rs 292,500. Content: faulty shirts 800 → 350 a month; saving Rs 292,500 a month v one-off cost Rs 250,000 (pays back in under a month); reputation with buyers, motivation; reliability of the training company's claim, staff turnover, lost production time; monitoring fault rates. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Hamza Garments, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Hamza Garments, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem: MediLab Pharmaceuticals makes tablets. At present inspectors test samples at the end of production. Last week 4,800 boxes were made and 120 boxes were rejected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of boxes rejected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between quality control and quality assurance. Do you think MediLab should change to quality assurance? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Quality control: inspectors check finished products (or samples) at the end and remove faulty ones. Quality assurance: every worker checks quality at each stage, preventing faults. For MediLab, faulty medicines are dangerous; 2.5% rejects is costly waste, and sampling may miss faults that reach patients. QA cuts waste and risk, but needs training and time. Judgement: yes, because for medicines safety and reputation are critical; keep some final testing too.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: correct difference (end inspection v at every stage/prevention). Up to 2 marks: analysis applied to medicines and the reject rate. Up to 2 marks: justified judgement.

practice.stem: Ayesha wants to start a mobile app business in Karachi that helps families book home tutors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two characteristics of a successful entrepreneur.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. willing to take risks; creative/innovative; hard-working; self-confident; good communicator; determined/resilient; able to plan and organise.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items Ayesha should include in her business plan.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. description of the business idea and objectives; market research findings and target market; marketing plan (price, promotion); finance needed and sources; cash-flow forecast and forecast profit; details of the owner and staff; location.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Business size can be measured in several ways.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two methods of measuring the size of a business, other than the number of employees.
parts.answer: Any two: value of output; capital employed; market share; sales revenue (value of sales).
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'internal growth'.
parts.answer: When a business expands its existing operations, for example by opening new branches or increasing output, using its own resources rather than joining with other businesses.
parts.working: 1 mark: expanding existing operations. 1 mark: not by merger or takeover / organic growth.

practice.stem:
The following decisions have been made by different businesses:
1 A flour mill buys a chain of bakeries.
2 A clothing retailer merges with another clothing retailer.
3 A dairy company buys the farms that supply its milk.
4 A cement company buys a chain of hotels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of integration shown in each of the four decisions.
parts.answer: 1 Forward vertical integration; 2 Horizontal integration; 3 Backward vertical integration; 4 Conglomerate integration (diversification).
parts.working: 1 mark each. For 1 and 3, accept 'vertical' for the mark only if forward/backward is correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one advantage to the dairy company of decision 3.
parts.answer: e.g. secure supply of milk, so it can control the quality and cost of milk and is not affected by supplier shortages.
parts.working: 1 mark for the advantage, 1 mark for development.

practice.stem:
The table shows information about two businesses.
Business A (a call centre): 120 employees; capital employed PKR 80 million
Business B (a chemical plant): 45 employees; capital employed PKR 150 million

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital employed per employee for each business, correct to the nearest PKR 1,000. Show your working.
parts.answer: Business A: PKR 667,000; Business B: PKR 3,333,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it can be misleading to compare these two businesses using only the number of employees.
parts.answer: Business A looks larger by employees, but Business B is capital-intensive (uses expensive machinery) and is larger by capital employed; different industries use different mixes of labour and capital.
parts.working: 1 mark: B is larger by capital employed / capital-intensive. 1 mark: industries differ in labour intensity.

practice.stem: Bilal opened a café in Islamabad six months ago. Sales have been lower than he expected and he is worried that the business might fail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of support available to people starting a business.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. government grants or low-interest loans; business advice and training schemes; business incubators/business parks; banks' small-business advisers; mentoring from experienced entrepreneurs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why new businesses such as Bilal's café often fail.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Lack of market research: Bilal may have chosen a location or menu that customers do not want, so sales are too low to cover rent. 2) Poor cash-flow management: he may run out of cash to pay suppliers and staff even if the café could become profitable. Other: strong competition from established cafés; lack of management experience; too little capital; changes in the market.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: Gul Khan runs a tailoring shop in Peshawar with two employees. He has run the business for 15 years and has no plans to expand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Gul Khan's business may stay small.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Owner's objectives: Gul Khan may be happy with his income and want to keep control and avoid stress, so he chooses not to grow. 2) Small market: tailored clothing is a personal service and customers want individual attention from a local tailor, so demand is limited to his area. Other: lack of finance for expansion; a skilled personal service is difficult to scale.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages to customers of buying from a small business.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. personal service; flexibility to meet individual needs; owner knows customers; local and convenient.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Nadia wants to borrow PKR 3 million from a bank to open a beauty salon in Faisalabad. The bank has asked her for a business plan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'business plan'.
parts.answer: A written document that describes a business, its objectives and how it will achieve them, including marketing, production and financial plans.
parts.working: 1 mark: written document. 1 mark: sets out the business's objectives/strategies and forecasts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Nadia of writing a business plan.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Easier to get finance: the bank can see forecast revenue and how Nadia will repay the PKR 3 million, so it is more likely to lend. 2) Reduces risk of failure: planning makes Nadia research customers, competitors and costs before she spends money, so she can spot problems early. Other: gives clear aims to measure progress against; helps her to persuade suppliers or partners.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: Two mobile network companies in the same country have merged to form one large company.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a merger and a takeover.
parts.answer: A merger is when two businesses agree to join together to form one business; a takeover is when one business buys enough shares to gain control of another.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems the merged company might face.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Different cultures: managers and staff from the two companies may have different ways of working, causing conflict and lower productivity. 2) Redundancies: duplicate shops and offices are closed, causing poor morale and possibly strikes. Other: diseconomies of scale – communication is slower in a much larger organisation; customers may lose choice and complain to the government; integrating IT networks is costly.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: Pak Biscuits Ltd makes biscuits. It plans to grow by buying one of its rival biscuit manufacturers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two benefits to a business of growth.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. economies of scale (lower average costs); larger market share; higher profits; more power over suppliers; less risk of being taken over.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think horizontal integration is the best way for Pak Biscuits Ltd to grow? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: quick increase in market share and fewer competitors; economies of scale in buying flour, sugar and packaging; gains the rival's brands and factory. Against: costly to buy the rival; cultural clashes; may need redundancies; competition authorities may object; risk is concentrated in one product. Alternatives: internal growth (cheaper, less risky but slow); vertical integration (secures supply of flour). Judgement, e.g. yes, because it quickly gains market share and lower costs, provided the price paid is not too high.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

practice.stem:
Bread Basket owns 8 bakeries in Lahore and wants to expand. It is considering two options.
Option 1 – internal growth: open 3 new bakeries, costing PKR 25 million each. Forecast annual profit: PKR 6 million per new bakery.
Option 2 – take over Golden Oven, a rival with 5 bakeries, for PKR 110 million. Golden Oven's annual profit is PKR 20 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Bread Basket choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, forecast annual profit as a percentage of the cost of each option).
parts.answer: Calculations: Option 1: 24.0%; Option 2: 18.2%. Option 1: higher return (24.0%), cheaper (PKR 75 m), keeps Bread Basket's own culture and quality, but slower and the forecast profit for new bakeries is uncertain. Option 2: lower return (18.2%) and costs PKR 110 m, but gains 5 bakeries at once with a known profit record, removes a competitor and gives more market share; may bring integration problems. Judgement, e.g. Option 1, because it gives a higher return for less money, unless Bread Basket needs to grow quickly to block competitors.
parts.working: Calculations: Option 1: (3 × 6) ÷ (3 × 25) × 100 = 18 ÷ 75 × 100 = 24.0%. Option 2: 20 ÷ 110 × 100 = 18.2%. Content: Option 1 = 18 ÷ 75 × 100 = 24.0%; Option 2 = 20 ÷ 110 × 100 = 18.2%; internal growth cheaper and keeps culture/quality but slower and forecast uncertain; takeover gives 5 bakeries at once with a known profit record, removes a rival, more market share, but integration problems and higher cost. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Bread Basket, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Bread Basket, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem:
Zain plans to open a juice bar in Multan and wants a bank loan of PKR 6 million. His business plan contains these monthly forecasts:
Juices sold: 300 per day, 26 days a month; price PKR 350 per juice
Ingredient cost: PKR 120 per juice
Rent PKR 250,000; wages PKR 400,000; other fixed costs PKR 144,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Do you think the bank should lend Zain the PKR 6 million? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: PKR 1,000,000. For: forecast profit of PKR 1 m a month (PKR 12 m a year) would easily cover repayments; plan shows he has thought about costs. Against: forecasts may be optimistic – 300 juices every day may be unrealistic for a new business, especially in winter; no evidence of market research or competitors; Zain's experience unknown; the loan is large and he may have no collateral. Judgement, e.g. lend only if Zain shows market research supporting the sales forecast and offers security, because profit is very sensitive to the number of juices sold.
parts.working: Calculations: revenue 300 × 26 × 350 = 2,730,000; ingredients 300 × 26 × 120 = 936,000; fixed costs 794,000. 2,730,000 − 936,000 − 794,000 = PKR 1,000,000. Content: revenue PKR 2.73 m, ingredients PKR 0.936 m, fixed costs PKR 0.794 m, forecast profit PKR 1 m a month (PKR 12 m a year); repayments easily covered if forecasts are right; but 300 juices a day may be optimistic (new business, winter), no market research or competitor evidence, experience and collateral unknown; profit very sensitive to sales. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to the bank's decision about Zain, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to the bank's decision about Zain, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem: Saleem is a sole trader who runs a mobile phone repair shop in Quetta.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'unlimited liability'.
parts.answer: The owner is personally responsible for all the debts of the business, so personal possessions can be taken to pay them if the business fails.
parts.working: 1 mark: owner responsible for all business debts. 1 mark: personal assets at risk.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages to Saleem of being a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. easy and cheap to set up; Saleem keeps all the profit; he has full control and makes decisions quickly; financial information stays private; flexible working.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Many businesses in Pakistan are organised as companies or franchises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'franchise'.
parts.answer: A business arrangement where the franchisor gives the franchisee the right to use its brand name, logo and business methods in return for a fee and/or a share of sales (royalty).
parts.working: 1 mark: right to use another business's name/brand/methods. 1 mark: in return for a fee or royalty.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of a public limited company.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. shares can be sold to the general public, e.g. on the stock exchange; shareholders have limited liability; separate legal identity; must publish its accounts; owned by shareholders and run by directors.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Dr Farah and Dr Imran are dentists. They plan to set up a dental clinic together in Lahore as a partnership.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'partnership agreement'.
parts.answer: A written legal document setting out the terms of a partnership, such as how much capital each partner invests, how profits are shared and what happens if a partner leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark: written/legal agreement between partners. 1 mark: an example of what it contains.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages to the dentists of forming a partnership instead of each operating as a sole trader.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) More capital: both dentists invest, so they can afford expensive dental chairs and X-ray equipment. 2) Shared workload and skills: they can cover each other's patients during holidays or illness, and one could specialise in children's dentistry, attracting more patients. Other: shared decision-making; losses shared.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: Rizwan runs a successful furniture shop in Islamabad as a sole trader. He plans to borrow money to open a large showroom and is thinking of forming a private limited company with his brother.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages to Rizwan of forming a private limited company.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Limited liability: if the large showroom fails, Rizwan would only lose the money he invested, not his house or savings. 2) More capital: he can sell shares to his brother (and other family or friends) to raise finance for the showroom. Other: separate legal identity, so the company continues if an owner dies; may appear more creditworthy to suppliers and banks.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one disadvantage of a private limited company compared with a sole trader.
parts.answer: e.g. more legal formalities and costs to set up and run; accounts must be filed and are less private; profits shared with other shareholders; Rizwan loses some control.
parts.working: 1 mark for the disadvantage, 1 mark for brief development.

practice.stem: QuickBite is a burger chain with 30 outlets run by franchisees. Each franchisee pays QuickBite a royalty of 6% of sales revenue. One franchisee in Rawalpindi had sales revenue of PKR 24 million last year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the royalty paid to QuickBite by the Rawalpindi franchisee. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to QuickBite (the franchisor) of growing by franchising.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Low-cost growth: franchisees pay to open their outlets, so QuickBite can expand to 30 outlets without raising large amounts of capital. 2) Regular income: QuickBite receives royalties (e.g. PKR 1.44 m from one outlet) with less risk than running the outlets itself. Other: franchisees are motivated owners, so outlets are well run; brand awareness grows.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point). Answers about benefits to the franchisee gain no marks.

practice.stem: Hassan Foods Ltd is a family-owned private limited company that makes cooking oil. The directors are considering becoming a public limited company to raise finance for a new refinery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one reason why a public limited company can usually raise more capital than a private limited company.
parts.answer: It can sell shares to the general public on the stock exchange, so many more investors can buy shares.
parts.working: 1 mark: sells shares to the public. 1 mark: on the stock exchange / much larger pool of investors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Hassan Foods Ltd should become a public limited company? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: raises large amounts of capital for the refinery without interest payments; higher status helps with suppliers and banks; shares easy to sell. Against: the family may lose control if outsiders buy many shares, including risk of takeover; costly and complicated to convert; must publish detailed accounts; shareholders may want short-term dividends. Judgement, e.g. yes if the family keeps more than half of the shares and the refinery cannot be financed by loans; otherwise use a bank loan to keep control.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

practice.stem: Omar wants to open a fried-chicken restaurant in Karachi. He could open it under his own brand, or buy a franchise from an international chain. The franchise would cost an initial fee of $40,000 plus a royalty of 5% of sales each year. Omar forecasts first-year sales of $300,000. He has never run a restaurant before.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Omar buy the franchise or open under his own brand? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: $55,000. Franchise: well-known brand attracts customers from the first day; training and support useful as Omar has no restaurant experience; proven menu and suppliers; banks may lend more readily. But costs $55,000 in year 1 and royalties every year; less control over menu, prices and decor; must follow franchisor rules. Own brand: keeps all profit and full control, but higher risk of failure and must build customer awareness. Judgement, e.g. franchise, because Omar's lack of experience makes failure likely without support, and the brand reduces risk despite the $55,000 cost.
parts.working: Calculations: royalty 5% × 300,000 = $15,000. 40,000 + 15,000 = $55,000. Content: first-year payment 40,000 + 5% × 300,000 = $55,000; franchise — known brand, training and support for an inexperienced owner, proven menu and suppliers, easier bank loans, but fees every year and less control; own brand — keeps all profit and control, but higher risk of failure and must build awareness. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Omar, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Omar, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem: Mehran Motors is a private sector car parts manufacturer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two objectives that a private sector business might have.
parts.answer: Any two: survival; profit; growth; increasing market share; social/ethical objectives (e.g. helping the community).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'stakeholder'.
parts.answer: Any person or group with an interest in the activities and performance of a business.
parts.working: 1 mark: person or group. 1 mark: with an interest in/affected by the business.

practice.stem:
The following groups have an interest in Faisal Textiles:
employees; customers; shareholders; the local community; managers; the government

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the six groups as an internal or an external stakeholder.
parts.answer: Internal: employees, shareholders (owners), managers. External: customers, the local community, the government.
parts.working: 4 marks for all six correct; 3 for five; 2 for four; 1 for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one objective that customers of Faisal Textiles might have.
parts.answer: e.g. good-quality cloth at reasonable prices / reliable delivery / good after-sales service.
parts.working: 2 marks for a clear objective; 1 mark for a vague one.

practice.stem: Sapphire Paints plans to extend its factory near a residential area in Gujranwala. The extension will double output and create 80 new jobs, but will increase lorry traffic and fumes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two stakeholder groups that would support the factory extension.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. shareholders (higher profit); managers (business growth); unemployed local people/workers (more jobs); government (more tax, jobs); suppliers (more orders).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two conflicts between stakeholder objectives that the extension might cause.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Shareholders vs local community: shareholders want higher profits from doubled output, but residents want clean air and quiet roads, so they may protest and delay planning permission. 2) Workers vs shareholders: new jobs are welcome, but workers may want higher wages from the increased profits while shareholders want higher dividends. Other: customers want low prices vs owners want high profit; government wants jobs but also environmental protection.
parts.working: For each conflict: 1 mark for the two groups/objectives, 1 mark for application, 1 mark for development.

practice.stem: Roshni Solar is a social enterprise in Sindh. It sells low-cost solar lamps to villages without electricity and trains local women to sell and repair them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'social enterprise'.
parts.answer: A business that has social objectives, such as helping people or the environment, as well as making a profit, and uses most of its profit to meet those social aims.
parts.working: 1 mark: business with social/environmental objectives. 1 mark: also needs profit / reinvests profit in its aims.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two objectives Roshni Solar is likely to have.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Social: provide light to homes without electricity so children can study at night and families stop using dangerous kerosene lamps. 2) Economic: make enough profit to survive and expand to more villages, and provide income for the local women it trains. 3) Environmental: reduce pollution by replacing kerosene with solar power.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: Fizz Up is a new soft-drinks business. In its first year it had sales of PKR 4.2 million in a market where total sales were PKR 35 million. It made a small loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Fizz Up's market share. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think profit should be the most important objective for Fizz Up at this stage? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For profit: needs profit for long-term survival and to repay loans; owners want a return. Against: as a new business, survival is more important – it must build cash flow and customers first; increasing market share (already 12%) and brand awareness may require low prices and heavy advertising that reduce short-term profit; profit becomes more important later. Judgement, e.g. no – survival and market share matter more now, because a new drinks brand must win customers from established brands before it can earn profit; objectives change as the business grows.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

practice.stem: Sana makes celebration cakes at home in Lahore. The ingredients and box for one cake cost PKR 750, and she sells the cake for PKR 1,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'added value'.
parts.answer: The difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials and components used to make it.
parts.working: 1 mark: selling price minus. 1 mark: cost of bought-in materials/components.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the added value of one cake. Show your working.

practice.stem: Al-Haq Motors assembles cars on a production line where each worker does one task, such as fitting doors or installing seats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'specialisation'.
parts.answer: When people, businesses, regions or countries concentrate on what they are best at producing, for example workers concentrating on one task (division of labour).
parts.working: 1 mark: concentrating on one task/product. 1 mark: what they are best at / division of labour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Al-Haq Motors of specialisation on its production line.
parts.answer: Advantage: each worker becomes skilled and quick at one task, so more cars are assembled per day and the cost per car falls. Disadvantage: the work is repetitive and boring, so workers may be demotivated, make mistakes or leave; also, if one worker is absent, the whole line may stop.
parts.working: Advantage: 1 identify, 1 apply, 1 develop. Disadvantage: 1 identify, 1 apply, 1 develop.

practice.stem: Hill Valley Tea buys loose tea for PKR 1,100 per kg. It packs it into branded 250 g packs which sell for PKR 520 each. The packaging for each pack costs PKR 40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the added value per kg of tea. Show your working.
parts.answer: PKR 820 per kg
parts.working: M1: 4 packs per kg: selling price 4 × 520 = PKR 2,080; bought-in costs 1,100 + 4 × 40 = PKR 1,260. A1: 2,080 − 1,260 = PKR 820.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways Hill Valley Tea could increase its added value.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Stronger branding and advertising, e.g. stressing that the tea comes from hill gardens, so customers will pay a higher price per pack without costs rising much. 2) Attractive or premium packaging, e.g. gift tins, which allows a much higher price than the extra packaging cost. Other: add flavours (cardamom, green tea) to create premium products; reduce the cost of bought-in materials by buying in bulk; sell directly online at a higher price.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: Print Pro, a printing business in Karachi, has PKR 10 million to invest. It can either buy a new digital printing machine, expected to add PKR 2.2 million to profit each year, or buy two delivery vans, expected to save PKR 1.6 million a year in courier costs. It can afford only one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'opportunity cost'.
parts.answer: The next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.
parts.working: 1 mark: next best alternative. 1 mark: given up/forgone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Print Pro chooses the printing machine. State the opportunity cost of this decision and explain why opportunity cost is important when Print Pro makes decisions.
parts.answer: Opportunity cost: the two delivery vans (and the PKR 1.6 million a year saving they would have brought). It is important because resources are scarce; comparing the benefit given up helps Print Pro choose the option with the greatest benefit (here PKR 2.2 m is more than PKR 1.6 m), although it should also consider risk and non-financial factors such as reliable delivery.
parts.working: 1 mark: vans/the saving forgone. Up to 3 marks for explanation: scarce resources (1); compare benefits of alternatives (1); development using the figures or a non-financial factor (1).

practice.stem: Businesses can be classified into three sectors of economic activity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'primary sector'.
parts.answer: The sector of the economy that extracts natural resources, such as farming, fishing, mining and forestry.
parts.working: 1 mark: extracting/using natural resources. 1 mark: example(s).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sector for each of these businesses: a fish farm in Thatta; a bank in Islamabad; a fertiliser factory in Multan; a coal mine in Balochistan.
parts.answer: Fish farm – primary; bank – tertiary; fertiliser factory – secondary; coal mine – primary.
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

practice.stem:
The table shows the number of workers (in millions) in each sector in Country Z.
2005: primary 18; secondary 6; tertiary 6
2025: primary 15; secondary 10; tertiary 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of workers employed in the primary sector in 2005 and in 2025. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the importance of the tertiary sector has grown in Country Z.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Rising incomes: as people become richer they spend more on services such as restaurants, banking, education and tourism, creating more service jobs. 2) Mechanisation of farming: fewer workers are needed in agriculture, so people move to towns to work in services. Other: growth of IT and telecoms; tourism; global outsourcing of call centres.
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

practice.stem: The government of a country owns the national railway. It is losing money, and some politicians want to sell it to private sector businesses (privatisation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the public sector and the private sector.
parts.answer: Public sector businesses are owned and controlled by the government; private sector businesses are owned by private individuals or shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark for each sector correctly described. Do not accept 'private limited company' as a definition of the private sector.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think the railway should be privatised? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: private owners aim for profit, so may cut waste and improve efficiency; may invest more in new trains; government stops paying for losses and receives money from the sale. Against: private owners may close unprofitable routes that villages depend on; fares may rise; safety may be reduced to cut costs; the railway is a strategic service that benefits society (external benefits such as less road congestion). Judgement, e.g. privatise only with government rules on fares, safety and keeping essential routes, because efficiency gains are useful but the social service must be protected.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

practice.stem: Margalla Cement operates a large cement plant near a village in northern Punjab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'external cost'.
parts.answer: A cost of a business's activity that is paid by people or groups outside the business (society), not by the business itself.
parts.working: 1 mark: a cost resulting from the business's activity. 1 mark: borne by third parties/society, not the business.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two external costs that Margalla Cement's plant might create for the village.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. dust/air pollution causing breathing problems; noise from machinery; heavy lorries damaging local roads and causing congestion; damage to farmland or water supplies; loss of natural landscape from quarrying.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Pine View is a hotel in Murree that attracts many tourists every summer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'sustainable development'.
parts.answer: Development that meets the needs of people today without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
parts.working: 1 mark: meeting present needs. 1 mark: without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two ways Pine View could reduce its impact on the environment.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. install solar panels / energy-saving lighting; reuse towels to save water and detergent; recycle waste; stop using single-use plastic; buy food from local suppliers; harvest rainwater.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A pressure group is campaigning against a drinks company that sells water in single-use plastic bottles in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'pressure group'.
parts.answer: An organisation of people with a common interest who try to influence the decisions of businesses or the government.
parts.working: 1 mark: group of people with a shared interest/cause. 1 mark: tries to influence business or government decisions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two methods the pressure group could use to influence the drinks company.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. organising a consumer boycott; protests or demonstrations; social media campaigns and bad publicity; petitions; lobbying the government to pass laws.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The government has built a new metro bus line through the centre of Lahore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'external benefit'.
parts.answer: A gain from an activity that is received by people or groups outside the organisation carrying out the activity.
parts.working: 1 mark: a benefit/gain from an activity. 1 mark: received by third parties/society.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two external benefits of the new metro bus line.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. less road congestion as people leave their cars; less air pollution; shorter journey times so workers reach jobs more easily; more customers for shops near stations; new jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Evergreen Oils produces palm oil on plantations in Malaysia. An environmental pressure group says the company is cutting down rainforest to plant more palm trees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways the government could control the environmental impact of Evergreen Oils.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. laws banning or limiting forest clearance; fines for illegal clearing; taxes on environmental damage; permits/licences for land use; subsidies for sustainable farming.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways the pressure group's campaign could affect Evergreen Oils.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Boycott: food manufacturers and consumers may stop buying its palm oil, so sales and profit fall. 2) Bad publicity: the company's reputation is damaged, making it harder to attract investors or win contracts, and it may need to spend on public relations. 3) The company may change its methods, e.g. replanting forest, which raises costs but may later improve its image.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: The provincial government has introduced a pollution tax of PKR 1.50 per brick on brick kilns that still use old, smoky technology. Shah Bricks produces 600,000 bricks a month using the old technology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the monthly pollution tax Shah Bricks must pay. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways the pollution tax could affect Shah Bricks.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Higher costs: the PKR 900,000 a month reduces profit unless it raises brick prices, which may lose customers to cleaner kilns. 2) Incentive to change: the owner may invest in cleaner (zig-zag) kiln technology to avoid the tax; this needs finance now but saves tax and improves its image. Other: may cut output or workers.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: Northway Fashion is a clothing retailer in the UK. A newspaper reports that one of its suppliers uses child labour. Another supplier, which follows strict labour standards, charges more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'ethical decision'.
parts.answer: A decision based on what is morally right, rather than only on what makes the most profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: based on moral principles/doing what is right. 1 mark: may not maximise profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Northway Fashion might choose the more expensive supplier.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Reputation: continuing with a supplier using child labour could lead to boycotts and lost sales, so paying more protects long-term revenue. 2) Marketing advantage: it can advertise ethically made clothes, attracting customers willing to pay higher prices. Other: avoids legal action; attracts staff and investors who value ethics.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem:
A government is deciding whether to build a new international airport outside a city. The following effects have been identified:
1 Construction cost paid by the airport company
2 Noise for families living nearby
3 New jobs for local people in hotels and taxis
4 Wages paid by the airport company to its own staff
5 Loss of farmland and wildlife habitat
6 Shorter journey times for business travellers from the whole region

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the six effects as a private cost, an external cost, or an external benefit.
parts.answer: Private costs: 1 and 4. External costs: 2 and 5. External benefits: 3 and 6.
parts.working: 4 marks for all six correct; 3 marks for five; 2 marks for four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the government might approve the airport even though it creates external costs.
parts.answer: The government considers the total social costs and benefits; if the external benefits (jobs, faster travel, growth) plus private benefits are greater than all the costs, society as a whole gains.
parts.working: 1 mark: compare social benefits with social costs. 1 mark: development, e.g. benefits outweigh costs so society gains.

practice.stem: Green Leaf Tea Company buys tea from farmers in Sri Lanka. It pays farmers above the market price and uses only recyclable packaging. Its shareholders want higher profits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one way ethical behaviour could increase Green Leaf's sales.
parts.answer: e.g. Customers who care about fair treatment of farmers may choose Green Leaf over rival brands, increasing sales and allowing a higher price.
parts.working: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for development in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think acting ethically will reduce Green Leaf's profits? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Reduce: paying above market prices and recyclable packaging raise costs; if prices cannot rise, profit margins fall; price-sensitive customers may buy cheaper tea. Not reduce: stronger brand image and loyalty; can charge a premium price; reliable supply from loyal farmers; avoids bad publicity. Judgement, e.g. in the short run profit may fall, but in the long run it may rise if customers value ethical tea; it depends on how many customers will pay more.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

practice.stem: Bean There is a chain of coffee shops in Karachi. It buys 20,000 kg of coffee beans a year from Supplier X at $4.50 per kg. Supplier X has been accused of paying workers very low wages. Supplier Y is a certified fair-trade supplier that charges 12% more per kg. Bean There's customers are mostly young professionals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Bean There switch to Supplier Y? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: $10,800. Switch: protects reputation; fair-trade logo can be used in promotion and may attract young professionals who care about ethics; may justify slightly higher prices; avoids risk of boycott. Stay: extra $10,800 a year raises costs and reduces profit; customers may not notice or pay more; Supplier X may improve. Judgement, e.g. switch, because the extra cost is small compared with the risk to the brand and could be covered by a very small price rise per cup.
parts.working: Calculations: 20,000 × 4.50 = $90,000. 12% × 90,000 = $10,800. Content: extra cost 12% × 20,000 × 4.50 = $10,800 a year; fair-trade logo in promotion, appeal to ethically minded young professionals, reputation and boycott risk, possible small price rise per cup; higher costs and lower profit, customers may not notice or pay more. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Bean There, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Bean There, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem: Kohinoor Spinning Mills pays PKR 2.1 million a month for electricity from the national grid. It could install solar panels on its roof for PKR 18 million. The panels would reduce its electricity bill by PKR 450,000 a month. The mills would need a bank loan to buy the panels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Kohinoor Spinning Mills install the solar panels? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: 40 months. For: saves PKR 5.4 m a year; cost recovered in 40 months (about 3 years 4 months) and panels last much longer; less pollution so better image with buyers; protects against rising grid prices and power cuts. Against: PKR 18 m loan means interest costs; savings may be less on cloudy days; money cannot be used for new machinery (opportunity cost). Judgement, e.g. install, because savings repay the cost in just over 3 years while panels last far longer, as long as loan interest is affordable.
parts.working: Calculations: 18,000,000 ÷ 450,000. 40 months. Content: payback 18,000,000 ÷ 450,000 = 40 months; saving PKR 5.4 m a year; panels last much longer than the payback; protection from grid price rises and power cuts; image with buyers; loan interest; lower output on cloudy days; opportunity cost (machinery). Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Kohinoor Spinning Mills, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Kohinoor Spinning Mills, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

practice.stem: AutoPak assembles cars in Karachi. The government and customers are increasingly concerned about the environment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways AutoPak could make its cars more environmentally friendly.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. produce hybrid or electric cars; improve fuel efficiency; use recycled materials; reduce weight; fit cleaner engines meeting emission standards.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two environmental issues AutoPak faces. Which is likely to be the most important to AutoPak? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Air pollution from cars and the factory: stricter emission laws may force costly redesigns and fines. Waste and resource use: disposal of old parts and use of steel and plastics raises costs and attracts criticism. Other: energy use in the factory; pressure groups. Judgement, e.g. air pollution, because government emission rules affect whether AutoPak can legally sell its cars, so it directly affects sales.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each issue (knowledge + analysis). 2 marks for a justified choice explaining why the other issue is less important.

practice.stem: Many Pakistani consumers now buy products made in China, the USA and Europe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'globalisation'.
parts.answer: The increasing freedom of movement of goods, services, capital and people between countries, so that the world acts more like one market.
parts.working: 1 mark: growing trade/links between countries. 1 mark: movement of goods, capital or people / world becoming one market.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons for the growth of globalisation.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. fewer trade barriers due to free trade agreements; cheaper and faster transport (container ships, air freight); improved communications and the internet; growth of multinational companies; industrialisation of developing countries.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A Japanese motorcycle company has opened a factory in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'multinational company'.
parts.answer: A business that has factories, production or service operations in more than one country.
parts.working: 1 mark: business operating/producing. 1 mark: in more than one country (not just selling there).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits to Pakistan of the multinational opening the factory.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. creates jobs; workers gain new skills; government receives more tax revenue; increases exports; brings new technology; more choice of products for consumers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The government of a country wants to protect its local shoe makers from cheap imported shoes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'import tariff'.
parts.answer: A tax placed on goods brought into a country.
parts.working: 1 mark: tax. 1 mark: on imported goods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'import quota'.
parts.answer: A limit on the quantity (number or volume) of a good that can be imported into a country.
parts.working: 1 mark: limit/restriction. 1 mark: on the physical quantity of imports.

practice.stem: Sialkot Sports makes footballs that it exports to the USA. It charges PKR 3,360 per football. The exchange rate is $1 = PKR 280.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price of one football in US dollars at this exchange rate. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The exchange rate changes to $1 = PKR 260 and Sialkot Sports keeps its price at PKR 3,360. Calculate the new price in US dollars, correct to 2 decimal places, and state whether the rupee has appreciated or depreciated.
parts.answer: $12.92; the rupee has appreciated
parts.working: B1: 3,360 ÷ 260 = $12.92. B1: appreciated (fewer rupees are needed to buy $1).

practice.stem: Pak Auto Assemblers in Karachi imports steel at $650 per tonne. The government has put a 15% tariff on imported steel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the tariff paid on each tonne of imported steel. Show your working.
parts.answer: $97.50 per tonne

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways the tariff could affect Pak Auto Assemblers.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Higher costs: steel costs $747.50 a tonne, raising the cost of each car; either price rises (fewer sales) or profit per car falls. 2) Change of supplier: it may buy steel from local mills instead, which could be cheaper now but may be lower quality or slower to deliver. Other: may need more working capital; competitiveness against imported cars may fall.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: Surgimed exports surgical instruments from Sialkot to the USA. A set of instruments is priced at PKR 8,700. The exchange rate changes from $1 = PKR 250 to $1 = PKR 290.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price in US dollars of a set before and after the exchange rate change. Show your working.
parts.answer: Before $34.80; after $30.00

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of the change in the exchange rate on Surgimed.
parts.answer: The rupee has depreciated. 1) Exports become cheaper for US buyers ($34.80 → $30.00), so Surgimed may sell more sets and gain market share. 2) Imported inputs such as special steel or machinery cost more in rupees, raising production costs and possibly reducing profit margins. Other: Surgimed could instead keep the dollar price and earn more rupees per set.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: A large Chinese electronics multinational plans to build a television factory in Kenya.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why the multinational might want to produce in Kenya.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. lower labour costs; to be closer to African markets and cut transport costs; to avoid import tariffs; government incentives/grants; access to raw materials.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two possible disadvantages to Kenya of the multinational building the factory.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Local TV makers may not be able to compete with the multinational's economies of scale and may close, so some local jobs are lost. 2) Profits may be sent back to China rather than reinvested in Kenya. Other: senior jobs filled by foreign managers; environmental damage; multinational may leave suddenly; may pressure the government for tax breaks.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

practice.stem: Chiniot Craft makes hand-carved wooden furniture and sells it in Pakistan. It is worried about globalisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one threat and one opportunity that globalisation creates for Chiniot Craft.
parts.answer: Threat: cheaper factory-made furniture imported from abroad may take customers, so Chiniot Craft's sales and profit fall unless it cuts costs or stresses its hand-made quality. Opportunity: it can sell online to customers abroad, for example in the Gulf or UK where buyers value hand-carved furniture, increasing sales and allowing higher prices.
parts.working: Threat: 1 identify, 1 apply, 1 develop. Opportunity: 1 identify, 1 apply, 1 develop. Other opportunities: import cheaper tools or materials; set up abroad.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one way Chiniot Craft could respond to more foreign competition.
parts.answer: e.g. focus on unique hand-carved designs and branding to differentiate from mass-produced imports.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid response, 1 mark for brief development.

practice.stem: Several multinational fast-food and drinks companies have opened outlets in Pakistan over the last 20 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one reason why a multinational company may be welcomed by the government of the host country.
parts.answer: e.g. It creates jobs, which reduces unemployment and increases income tax and spending in the economy.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think multinational companies are good for a country such as Pakistan? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Good: jobs, training and new skills; tax revenue; new technology; investment in infrastructure; more choice and better quality for consumers; may increase exports.
